title: B.C. inquest hears RCMP shooting victim died of shock and blood loss
article: The inquest into the RCMP shooting death of Donald Dwayne Lewis, 43, heard the victim died from shock and blood loss due to a gunshot wound to the chest.
Pathologist Dr. Darryl McNaughton told the inquest Tuesday it was physiologically possible for someone with a wound like Lewis's to continue fighting for several minutes.
Lewis died on Aug. 13, 2006, following an altercation with a Williams Lake RCMP officer near McLeese Lake, off Highway 97.
Constable Cole Brewer, 36, had responded to a woman's call about a suspicious man illegally camping on private property, the inquest heard.

On Monday, the inquest heard that Brewer got into a confrontation with Lewis and used his fists, baton and pepper spray, before shooting him once. Brewer said he handcuffed the injured Lewis to a tree while he went back to his car to radio for assistance. Lewis died while handcuffed to the tree.
McNaughton said someone with the type of injury Lewis had would likely die within 15 to 60 minutes.
McNaughton said applying pressure to the wound or simple first aid would not have been enough to save Lewis. He would have needed an immediate IV and surgery soon after.
The forensic pathologist testified there were no signs of alcohol or drugs in Lewis's system.

New details about Brewer's role were also revealed Tuesday. On the night of the shooting, Brewer's police partner was off for the night. The officer did not expect a confrontation when he responded to a call about a man camping on Crown land near a woman's home.
"I thought I'd be an arbitrator," Brewer told the inquest.
Brewer served as a NATO peacekeeper in Bosnia from 2002-2003 and in addition to supervising rebuilding projects, one of his duties was to seize AK-47s and grenades from the homes of civilians.
Brewer became a Mountie in 2005, and had served on the force for 18 months prior to the shooting.
Lawyer Cameron Ward, who represents Lewis's widow Sarah Lewis, told the inquest that Brewer received special treatment from RCMP investigators.
Ward pointed out that a dozen RCMP officers from Williams Lake, Brewer's co-workers and friends, were the first to secure the scene and investigate Lewis's death.

Ward questioned why police failed to test Brewer's gun for fingerprints, why he didn't give a statement for three days and why the officer was allowed to re-visit the scene of the shooting before he made a videotaped statement.
Ward told the jury that regular procedure was not followed, claiming Brewer was "treated vastly different than a civilian."
At the close of the inquest, which is expected to last two weeks, the jury will have the opportunity to make recommendations aimed at preventing deaths under similar circumstances in the future.
